AGENDA
  BUILDING AND FIRE BOARD OF APPEALS
  VIA TELECONFERENCE ONLY
 Welcome to the meeting of the Building and Fire Board of Appeals. Meetings are broadcast live on
 cable channel 6 (GTV6) and rebroadcast throughout the week. Call (818) 548-4013 for program
 schedules. DVDs of the proceedings are available for purchase in the City Clerk’s Office. Meetings
 are also archived on the City Website for viewing anytime at
 https://www.glendaleca.gov/government/public-meeting-portal. If you have any question about
 matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact the office of the Building Official
 at (818) 548-3214 during regular business hours.
  PLEASE TURN OFF CELLULAR PHONES WHILE INSIDE THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.
 In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, auxiliary hearing aids, sign
 language translation, and Braille transcripts are available upon request. Assisted listening devices
 are available same-day upon request. At least 48 hours (or two business days) notice is required
 for requests regarding sign language translation and Braille transcription services. All documents
 related to open session items on this agenda that are received less than 72 hours prior to this
 meeting, and are public records, will be available for review in the Office of the City Clerk, 613 E.
 Broadway, RM 110, Glendale, CA 91206.
 Translation services are provided for meetings through the use of bilingual staff for speakers who
 wish to utilize the service as available. Speakers should state their request by contacting the City
 Clerk’s office at (818) 548-2090, at least 24 hours prior to the scheduled meeting. Please specify
 the language for which you require translation. The exclusive use of City provided interpreters is not
 required and persons are welcome to use their own interpreter or speak in their native language.
  JUNE 16, 2021 AT 2:00 PM

Due to the evolving situation with the COVID-19 novel coronavirus and health recommendations from
the LA County Health Department, the Building and Fire Board of Appeals commission meeting will
be available to the public electronically.

Due to social distancing requirements, the public will not be able to attend the meeting. The public is
encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes to practice social distancing.

The meeting can be viewed:
On local cable: Charter Cable Channel 6 and AT&T U-verse Channel 99.
Streaming Online: https://www.glendaleca.gov/government/public-meeting-portal

For public comments and questions during the meeting call (818) 937-8100.
 City staff will be submitting these questions and comments in real time to the appropriate person
during the Building and Fire Board of Appeals commission meeting.

  INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMUNICATION

DATE:  June 16, 2021

TO:  Building and Fire Board of Appeals

FROM:  Loren Klick, Urban Forester

BY:  Katherine Williams, Arborist Technician

SUBJECT:  Indigenous Tree Pruning Permit Application Appeal, #BITO2016405

The following report summarizes Public Works’ position on the permit appeal case
under review. Please see the attached Appendix for additional documentation, including
copies of relevant emails, letters, and the permit application showing the protected
coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia) that is the subject of the pruning request.

SUMMARY
Public Works staff considers the core conflict of this case to be a private neighbor
dispute that must be resolved before the applicant re-submits a permit application to the
City for review.

The tree owner has let it be known to the applicant that he does not consent to the
removal of a large limb from the oak tree residing on his property. While the canopy of
this tree spans over the property line, the tree itself is considered the private property of
the tree owner. It is not the City’s right to “permit” work on private property without the
consent of the property owner.

Therefore, Public Works staff respectfully requests that the applicant and the tree owner
come to an understanding before re-submitting an Indigenous Tree Permit application
for review. The application to remove the limb may also be re-submitted in the future if
this limb is shown to be dead, hazardous, or otherwise meets the exemptions listed per
GMC 12.44.060.

  1|Page
 Case History
  • On June 23, 2020, Apers Tree Service contacted the Arborist Technician with the
  request to remove a large oak tree limb emanating from the neighboring property
  at 2245 Hollister Terrace, on behalf of the property owner at 2253 Hollister
  Terrace, Mr. Michael Barclay. After reviewing photographs and discussing the
  request with Apers Tree Service over the phone, the Arborist Technician gave
  preliminary approval to perform the pruning on the condition that the tree owner
  provided his signature on the permit application.
  • On August 21, 2020, the tree owner, Mr. Paul Yazaki, contacted the Arborist
  Technician to review the request before giving his final written signature on the
  permit application.
  • On August 26, 2020, Mr. Barclay contacted the Arborist Technician via email
  stating that he had received verbal approval from Mr. Yazaki to perform the
  pruning.
  • On September 1, 2020, the Arborist Technician and Mr. Yazaki met in person to
  discuss the Indigenous Tree Ordinance and the permit request.
  • On September 3, 2020, Mr. Barclay contacted the Arborist Technician via email
  again stating that he had received verbal approval from Mr. Yazaki to perform the
  pruning.
  • On September 23, 2020, Mr. Barclay contacted the Arborist Technician via email
  stating that Mr. Yazaki had recently informed him that he had changed his mind
  regarding his approval of the work and would not be signing the permit
  application.
  • On October 1, 2020, Mr. Barclay submitted the permit application for the pruning
  request without Mr. Yazaki’s signature.
  • On October 15, 2020, the Arborist Technician denied the permit request on the
  basis of the lack of approval from the tree owner.
  • On October 16, 2020, Mr. Barclay appealed the decision to the Urban Forester.
  • On November 3, 2020, the Urban Forester denied the permit appeal.
  • On November 6, 2020, Mr. Barclay appealed the decision to the Director of
  Public Works.
  • On February 8, 2021, The Director of Public Works denied the permit appeal.
  • On February 18, 2021, Mr. Barclay appealed the decision to the Building and Fire
  Board of Appeals.

Indigenous Tree Ordinance: Case Context
The indigenous Oak, Bay, and Sycamore trees within the city are natural aesthetic
resources which help define the character of the city. These trees are worthy of
protection in order to preserve the natural environment and to protect the city’s native
plant life heritage for the benefit of all residents. It is pertinent to the public interest,
  P a g e 2 | 13
 health and welfare that these trees be protected from mutilation, indiscriminate cutting,
damage, destruction or removal (GMC 12.44).

The Indigenous Tree Ordinance is designed to generally require a permit for pruning
work that is significant enough to potentially cause long term damage or total tree loss,
per the standard practices defined by the International Society of Arboriculture. The
benefits of the permit application review process include access to Public Works staff’s
arboricultural expertise, educational resources, and guidance on appropriate tree
protection measures and tree care as mandated by the Indigenous Tree Ordinance.

In general, a permit is not required when the proposed pruning is categorically minor,
and therefore unlikely to cause short or long term damage to the tree, or when safety
concerns supersede the permit process. These exemptions include, but are not limited
to:

  •  Cases of emergency caused by a protected indigenous tree being in a hazardous
  or dangerous condition and requiring immediate action.
  •  Emergency or routine cleaning by a public utility necessary to protect or maintain
  electrical, power or communication lines or other property of a public utility.
  •  Routine pruning involving the removal of any dead, dying, or diseased branches
  of a tree and the cutting of live interfering and weak branches not to exceed two
  (2) inches in diameter, performed in accordance with industry standards, and
  foliage reduction not to exceed one-quarter (1/4) of the total tree foliage.
  •  Any trimming of a tree performed to meet minimum clearance requirements for
  fire and life safety as set forth in a notice to abate fire hazard issued by the fire
  department. (GMC 12.44.060)

While all residents are encouraged to notify their neighbors of any tree work occurring at
their property line, please note that in the scenarios listed above, proof of the tree
owner’s approval of the proposed tree work is not required by the City since in these
cases no permit is required.

In the case of this tree trimming request, the proposed limb for reduction is between
eight to twelve inches in diameter and extends approximately 15 to 20 feet from the
tree’s main trunk, at approximately six to eight feet above the ground. The wide, lateral
branching structural exhibited by the subject oak tree is typical of the species, especially
for mature specimens that have been allowed to retain their natural shape. The
applicant is requesting that the limb be reduced by approximately 10 to 12 feet, which
would remove the majority of the existing foliage growing from this limb and retain
several small vertical branches that are sprouting from the limb closer to the property

  P a g e 3 | 13
 line between 2253 and 2245 Hollister Terrace. The pruning cut would be approximately
12 inches in diameter. Based on the size of the proposed pruning cut, the proposed
pruning must be performed with an Indigenous Tree Permit.

Public Works staff requires the signature of the tree owner on all pruning permit
applications because the City recognizes trees as the tree owner’s private property. It is
not the City’s right to “permit” work on private property without the consent of the
property owner. Therefore, Forestry staff requires that neighbors come to an
understanding before submitting an Indigenous Tree Permit application for review.

CONCLUSION
The Indigenous Tree Ordinance recognizes long term tree care and risk management
decisions as the tree owner’s responsibility. Trees are living organisms and are
sensitive to damage. Significant pruning in just one part of a tree’s canopy has the
potential to cause decay, decline, and even death of the entire tree over time, increase
the potential for limb or trunk failure, and cause other adverse effects. Therefore,
neighbors, tree contractors, or other agents of the tree owner are free to submit a tree
permit application on the owner’s behalf, on the condition that the signature of the tree
owner is included on the permit application showing their knowledge and approval of the
proposed work.

The Department of Public Works respectfully requests that the permit applicant, Mr.
Barclay, confirms that the tree owner, Mr. Yazaki, approves the proposed pruning work
before re-submitting the pruning application to Public Works staff. The application to
remove the limb may also be re-submitted in the future if this limb is shown to be dead,
hazardous, or otherwise meets the exemptions listed per GMC 12.44.060.
